literary_identity: Poet, polemicist, and Latin secretary to the Commonwealth; the author of Paradise Lost and the greatest English epic poet after Chaucer, whose career moved from lyric and masque through two decades of political prose to the late biblical epics and tragedies written in blindness.
biography: Born 9 December 1608 in London, son of a scrivener and composer; educated at St Paul's School and Christ's College, Cambridge (BA 1629, MA 1632), where he wrote his early odes and masques. After six years of private study at Horton (1632–38) producing 'L'Allegro', 'Il Penseroso', 'Comus', and 'Lycidas', he travelled in Italy (1638–39), meeting Galileo. From 1641 he threw himself into the Puritan cause, writing anti-prelatical tracts, the divorce pamphlets, Areopagitica (1644), and, after the regicide, The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates (1649) and Eikonoklastes; he served as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth under Cromwell, defending the republic in Latin (Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano, 1651). Totally blind by 1652, widowed twice, and imprisoned briefly at the Restoration, he composed and dictated Paradise Lost (1667), Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes (1671). He died 8 November 1674 in London.
literary_profile: The poet who claimed to write with 'no middle flight' and to 'justify the ways of God to men'; his career is the most consciously ambitious in English literature, yoking classical and Hebrew learning, republican politics, and Protestant faith to a grand style of Latinate blank verse.
stylistic_characteristics: Unrhymed blank verse of great sonority and extended periodic syntax; dense allusion to classical, biblical, and Renaissance sources; grand invocations and epic similes; a learned, muscular diction; and, in the prose, a fierce polemical vigour with sprawling, powerful sentences.
intellectual_concerns: Liberty of conscience, republicanism, and the defence of regicide; the problem of evil and free will; obedience and temptation; the fall and regeneration of mankind; the vocation of the poet as prophet and public teacher; marriage and divorce; the corruption of the church.
historical_significance: Paradise Lost is the supreme epic of the English language and reshaped English poetry and politics for three centuries; his prose tracts are foundational documents of free speech and republican theory, and his example defined the role of the poet as moral and political witness.
biographical_uncertainty: Milton's life is exceptionally well documented (Edward Phillips's and John Aubrey's early lives); the dating of Paradise Lost's composition and the precise nature of his blindness remain matters of scholarship.

literary_identity: Poet laureate, dramatist, critic, and translator; the dominant literary figure of the Restoration, who perfected the heroic couplet, founded modern English criticism and verse satire, and moved between Puritan, royalist, and Catholic allegiances with the times.
biography: Born 9 August 1631 at Aldwincle; educated at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1654). He supported Cromwell at his death (Heroic Stanzas, 1658) then hailed the Restoration (Astraea Redux, 1660). In London he married Lady Elizabeth Howard (1663), wrote heroic plays and comedies for the King's Company, became laureate and historiographer royal (1668), and defended the moderns and the English stage in An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668). His political satires Absalom and Achitophel (1681) and Mac Flecknoe (1682) and the religious poems Religio Laici (1682) and The Hind and the Panther (1687, after his conversion to Catholicism) mark his maturity. Deprived of his offices by the Protestant William III (1688), he turned to translation, producing the great Virgil (1697) and Fables Ancient and Modern (1700). He died 1 May 1700 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The versatile master of Restoration letters — playwright, laureate, critic, satirist, and translator — who established the heroic couplet as the standard medium of serious English poetry and created a durable critical vocabulary.
stylistic_characteristics: The balanced, pointed heroic couplet; conversational yet elevated diction; satiric wit and character portraiture; a critical prose of clarity and good sense; and a translational idiom that naturalized the classics into contemporary English.
intellectual_concerns: The nature and decorum of drama and poetry; the quarrel of the ancients and moderns; political legitimacy, party, and succession; religious faith and conversion; the craft of translation and the history of the language.
historical_significance: Dryden created the Augustan style that Pope and Johnson inherited, founded English literary criticism, and produced the greatest political verse satire of the century; his translations made the classics central to English literary culture.
biographical_uncertainty: Dryden's life is well recorded; his religious and political shifts are documented in his own poems and prefaces, though their sincerity has been debated.

literary_identity: Anglican priest and devotional poet; author of The Temple, the greatest work of English religious lyric, whose intricate forms enact the struggles and consolations of the soul in God's service.
biography: Born 1593 at Montgomery into the distinguished Herbert family, brother of Lord Herbert of Cherbury; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge (Fellow 1609, MA 1616), where he became Public Orator (1620). Patronized by James I, he hoped for court preferment, but on the king's death turned to the church, taking holy orders (1626) and the poor country rectory of Bemerton near Salisbury (1630). He served as a devoted parish priest ('the holy Mr Herbert') until his death from consumption on 1 March 1633, aged 39. The Temple was published posthumously in 1633 by his friend Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding.
literary_profile: The poet of the parish and the conscience, who made the plain country church the setting for a demanding, intimate, and formally inventive poetry of devotion, doubt, and surrender.
stylistic_characteristics: Metaphysical wit turned to religious use; shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'); emblematic simplicity; dramatic colloquy with God; puns, scriptural allusion, and a musical variety of stanza forms.
intellectual_concerns: The soul's relation to God; obedience, affliction, and consolation; the priesthood and pastoral care; the conflict between worldly ambition and spiritual calling; the discipline of prayer.
historical_significance: The Temple is the supreme achievement of English devotional verse, influencing Vaughan, Crashaw, Coleridge, and the twentieth-century religious poets; Herbert's marriage of metaphysical wit to Anglican humility made him the model of the priest-poet.
biographical_uncertainty: Herbert's life is documented by Izaak Walton's Life (1670); the dating of individual poems in The Temple is largely inferential.

literary_identity: Anglo-Welsh physician, royalist, and metaphysical devotional poet; author of Silex Scintillans, whose mystical nature-poetry and longing for eternity distinguish him among Herbert's followers.
biography: Born 1621 (baptised 16 April) at Newton St Bridget, twin brother of the alchemist Thomas Vaughan; educated privately and at Jesus College, Oxford, then trained in medicine. A royalist during the Civil Wars, he retired to his native Breconshire, practised medicine, and published Olor Iscanus (1651) and Silex Scintillans (1650, expanded 1655), influenced by Herbert. He also wrote prose devotional and hermetic works (The Mount of Olives, 1652) and translations of Nolle and Boece. He lived quietly through the Restoration at Newton and Alway, dying 23 April 1695.
literary_profile: The 'Silurist' whose verse seeks God through the natural world and childhood memory, marked by a mystic's sense of eternity glimpsed behind the material world ('intimations' later echoed by Wordsworth).
stylistic_characteristics: Luminous nature imagery; a mystical, visionary quality; Herbert's influence tempered by a wilder, more personal imagination; emblematic structure; and Welsh landscape as the locus of spiritual experience.
intellectual_concerns: Eternity and the soul's pre-existence; nature as the book of God; childhood innocence; royalism and religious loyalty; hermetic and alchemical philosophy; death and resurrection.
historical_significance: Long neglected, Vaughan was recovered in the nineteenth century and prized by the Romantics and T. S. Eliot as a visionary metaphysical poet; 'The Retreat' and 'The World' are among the great English mystical lyrics.
biographical_uncertainty: Much of Vaughan's life is obscure; his exact birth date and many details of his royalist activities and medical practice rest on inference and local records.

literary_identity: Metaphysical religious poet and Catholic convert; author of Steps to the Temple and Carmen Deo Nostro, whose ecstatic, sensuous, and baroque devotional verse — especially to St Teresa and the Virgin — is unique in English.
biography: Born c. 1613 in London, son of a Puritan preacher; educated at Charterhouse and Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (Fellow of Peterhouse). A Laudian Anglican, he was ejected during the Civil Wars, converted to Roman Catholicism, and went into exile, first to Paris and then to Italy. He became a client of Cardinal Palotta and, in 1649, a canon of the Holy House of Loreto, where he died in July 1649. His Steps to the Temple (1646) was published in England; the Catholic Carmen Deo Nostro appeared in Paris in 1652.
literary_profile: The English poet most at home in the continental baroque, whose fervent Catholic imagination rendered the mystical ecstasy of the saints in lush, sensuous, and sometimes startlingly physical conceits.
stylistic_characteristics: Baroque extravagance; sensuous and paradoxical imagery; the epigram and the witticism turned to devotion; musical repetition; and a Catholic and Counter-Reformation intensity alien to the Protestant mainstream.
intellectual_concerns: Mystical union and ecstasy; the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalene, and St Teresa; martyrdom and the wounds of Christ; the conversion of the soul; the sensuous apprehension of the divine.
historical_significance: Crashaw is the principal English representative of continental baroque religious poetry; his 'Hymn to St Teresa' and his epigrams were admired by Cowley and, later, by the decadents and modern critics as the most sensuously daring of the metaphysicals.
biographical_uncertainty: Crashaw's birth year (1612 or 1613) and the details of his conversion and exile are uncertain; his biography rests on scattered records and the testimony of Abraham Cowley.

literary_identity: Anglican priest, mystical prose writer, and poet, discovered only in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries; author of Centuries of Thankfulness and the Roman Forgeries, whose ecstatic celebration of innocent vision and divine felicity is unlike anything else in English.
biography: Born c. 1636–37 in Hereford, son of a shoemaker; educated at Brasenose College, Oxford (BA 1656–57), and ordained, holding the living of Credenhill near Hereford (1657–72) while serving as chaplain to Sir Orlando Bridgman at Teddington from 1669. He wrote prolifically in prose and verse but published little in his lifetime (only the anti-Catholic Roman Forgeries, 1673). He died of smallpox on 27 September 1674. His major works — Centuries of Thankfulness, The Kingdom of God, and the poems — circulated in manuscript and were misattributed to Vaughan until Bertram Dobell's editions of 1903–08 established his fame.
literary_profile: The mystic of felicity and wonder, who celebrated the infant soul's apprehension of the infinite in the world and argued that happiness consists in rightly valuing creation as God's gift.
stylistic_characteristics: A rhapsodic, cumulative prose of wonder and thanksgiving; long flowing 'centuries' or meditative paragraphs; visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood; and a lyric poetry of ecstatic innocence.
intellectual_concerns: Felicity and the desire for God; innocence and the vision of childhood; the infinity of the soul; gratitude and thanksgiving; the goodness of creation; free will and love.
historical_significance: Once unknown, Traherne is now recognised as a major mystical writer whose Centuries and poems anticipate Romantic and modernist celebrations of childhood vision and influenced figures from Christopher Smart to the twentieth century.
biographical_uncertainty: Traherne's birth year is uncertain (1636 or 1637); his manuscripts were long misattributed, and the dating and arrangement of his works remain subjects of scholarship.

literary_identity: Poet, essayist, and royalist secretary; the most celebrated English poet of the mid-seventeenth century, who adapted metaphysical wit, introduced the 'Pindaric' ode to English, and championed the new science and the plain prose style.
biography: Born 1618 in London, a posthumous son of a grocer; a child prodigy educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge, publishing Poetical Blossoms at fifteen (1633). A royalist, he served Queen Henrietta Maria in Paris (1646–56) as secretary and cipher-clerk, was imprisoned briefly on returning to England, and published his Poems (1656), including the Pindarique Odes, The Mistress, and Davideis. At the Restoration he was rewarded with the lease of Chertsey Abbey and a modest sinecure, wrote essays on retirement and the Royal Society (Of Plants, 1668), and died 28 July 1667. He was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer and Spenser.
literary_profile: The transitional figure between the metaphysicals and the Augustans, whose graceful verse, essays, and advocacy of the Royal Society made him the model of the cultivated Restoration man of letters.
stylistic_characteristics: Metaphysical conceit gradually disciplined toward neoclassical clarity; the irregular 'Pindaric' ode; fluent essayistic prose; and a witty, learned, but increasingly plain idiom.
intellectual_concerns: The value of retirement and the country life; the new experimental philosophy and Baconianism; biblical epic; love and poetic wit; the reform of prose style toward clarity.
historical_significance: Cowley's reputation stood above all his contemporaries' at the Restoration; his Pindaric odes created a major English form, his essays shaped the periodical and the plain style, and his advocacy of the Royal Society linked literature to the new science.
biographical_uncertainty: Cowley's life is well documented; the value of his poetry declined sharply after Johnson's Life exposed the 'violence' of his conceits, though modern criticism has revived interest.

literary_identity: Metaphysical and political poet, satirist, and long-serving Member of Parliament for Hull; author of 'To His Coy Mistress', 'Upon Appleton House', and the Horatian Ode, and of fierce Restoration prose satires against popery and arbitrary government.
biography: Born 31 March 1621 at Winestead, son of a Puritan clergyman; educated at Hull Grammar School and Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1639). He travelled abroad (1642–46), served as tutor to Mary Fairfax at Nun Appleton (1651–52), where he wrote several major poems, and to Lord Dutton's ward (1653–57). Elected MP for Hull in 1659, he held the post through the Restoration until his death, serving on the Council of State and defending religious toleration and the City of London's liberties. He wrote the prose satire The Rehearsal Transpros'd (1672–73) and An Account of the Growth of Popery (1677), and died suddenly on 16 August 1678. His Miscellaneous Poems were published posthumously in 1681.
literary_profile: The poet of balance and irony, who combined metaphysical wit with public conscience, writing equally as a lover, a country-house observer, a republican sympathiser, and a champion of toleration.
stylistic_characteristics: Tightly argued conceits and dramatic irony; the Horatian ode; satiric bite and wit; the country-house poem's topographical detail; and a prose of urbane, devastating irony and plain argument.
intellectual_concerns: Time, mortality, and desire; liberty of conscience and resistance to tyranny; the ethics of the estate and the country house; the corruption of court and clergy; the balance of wit and judgment.
historical_significance: Long valued only for a few lyrics, Marvell was re-established by T. S. Eliot as a major metaphysical poet and is now recognised as one of the greatest English lyric and political satirists, bridging the Interregnum and the Restoration.
biographical_uncertainty: Marvell's politics and even his religion were ambiguous in his lifetime and remain debated; most of his poems were published posthumously, so their dating is often inferential.

literary_identity: Court poet and politician, credited with perfecting the smooth closed heroic couplet and the Cavalier lyric; a long-lived figure whose verse was admired for its polish, melody, and gallantry from Charles I's court to the Restoration.
biography: Born 3 March 1606 at Coleshill, educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge. He entered Parliament and court society, celebrated Sacharissa (Lady Dorothy Sidney) in his lyrics, and was implicated in 'Waller's Plot' (1643) to secure London for the king, for which he was fined and banished. He returned under the Commonwealth, was elected to Parliament, and served through the Restoration with continued favour, revising his poems across a long career. He died 21 October 1687 at Beaconsfield.
literary_profile: The courtly lyricist whose 'smooth' verse and closed couplets became the model of elegant Restoration poetry; Dryden credited him with beginning 'the excellence of numbers' in English.
stylistic_characteristics: Melodious, polished, and balanced verse; the closed heroic couplet; gallant compliment and Petrarchan conceit refined to ease; panegyric and occasional poetry of public grace.
intellectual_concerns: Love and courtly compliment; royalist loyalty; the praise of patrons and the nation; the value of poetic polish and decorum; and, in later poems, time and old age.
historical_significance: Waller's technical refinement of the couplet directly shaped Denham, Dryden, and the whole Augustan line; though his reputation declined after the seventeenth century, he was the acknowledged father of smooth Restoration verse.
biographical_uncertainty: Waller's life is well recorded; the dating of individual lyrics and the identity of 'Sacharissa' are established, though many poems circulated in manuscript before print.

literary_identity: Cavalier poet, courtier, and soldier; the archetype of the gallant royalist gentleman whose lyrics of love, honour, and imprisonment — 'To Althea, from Prison' and 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars' — became the defining verse of the Cavalier cause.
biography: Born 1616 (baptised 10 December at St Bride's, London), educated at Charterhouse and Gloucester Hall, Oxford, and a favourite of the court of Charles I. He served in the Bishops' Wars and, in 1642, presented the Kentish petition for the restoration of episcopacy, for which he was imprisoned in the Gatehouse; a second imprisonment (1648–49) followed his loyalty after the Civil War, during which he prepared his collection Lucasta (1649). He spent his later years in poverty in London, publishing Lucasta: Posthume Poems (1659 was posthumous; actually published 1660). He died in 1657, reportedly in great poverty.
literary_profile: The Cavalier gentleman-poet whose code of honour made 'I could not love thee, dear, so much, / Loved I not honour more' the motto of royalist gallantry.
stylistic_characteristics: Elegant, musical lyrics; the argumentative conceit of love and honour; a gallant, dignified tone; and occasional metaphysical wit in the service of courtly feeling.
intellectual_concerns: Love and honour; loyalty to the king and the Cavalier cause; freedom of the spirit in imprisonment; friendship; and the consolation of poetry in defeat.
historical_significance: Lovelace's Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; his lyrics epitomise the royalist gentleman's ethos and remain among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: Lovelace's later life and the date and circumstances of his death are poorly documented; his reputation for a ruined, impoverished end rests partly on later tradition.

literary_identity: Cavalier lyric poet and courtier of Charles I's household; admired by his contemporaries as perhaps the finest of the Caroline wits, he combined Jonsonian polish with Donnean wit in short, intense love poems.
biography: Born c. 1595 at West Wickham, Kent, educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple. After a dissolute youth and service abroad (in the household of the ambassador at The Hague, from which he was dismissed for 'scurrility'), he became a server-in-ordinary to Charles I and moved in the court literary circle. His elegy 'An Elegy upon the Death of the Dean of Paul's, Dr John Donne' (1633) is a key document of the metaphysical transition. His Coelum Britannicum (masque, 1634) and his Poems were published in 1640, shortly before his death in 1639/40.
literary_profile: The consummate Caroline court lyricist, whose poems fuse sensual elegance with intellectual wit in a manner Clarendon called the 'muses' most delicate son'.
stylistic_characteristics: Polished, musical short lyrics; Donnean argument and conceit softened by Cavalier grace; sensuous wit; and a masterly control of the octosyllabic couplet.
intellectual_concerns: Love and desire; the pleasures and pains of courtship; poetry and immortality; the critique of Petrarchan convention; and courtly virtue.
historical_significance: Carew was ranked by contemporaries above most Cavalier poets; his synthesis of Donne and Jonson and his elegy on Donne make him central to understanding the metaphysical-to-Cavalier transition.
biographical_uncertainty: Carew's birth and death dates are approximate and his life poorly documented; most of his poems were printed posthumously in 1640.

literary_identity: Cavalier wit, courtier, and poet-playwright; famous for his rakish elegance, his sprightly songs, and his role as a dashing but ultimately tragic royalist, whose suicide in exile at thirty-three made him a legend of the Cavalier generation.
biography: Born February 1609 at Whitton, educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He inherited a large fortune, travelled Europe, served in the Bishops' Wars (raising a troop at his own expense), and became a celebrated figure of the court wits around the Earl of Holland and Thomas Hobbes. He wrote plays (Aglaura, 1638; The Goblins, 1638) and lyrics, and was knighted in 1630. He took part in the First Army Plot (1641) to rescue the Earl of Strafford, fled to Paris, and died there in June 1642, reportedly by his own hand after a servant's insult. His Fragmenta Aurea was published in 1646.
literary_profile: The most fashionable Cavalier wit, whose careless grace and easy songs ('Why so pale and wan, fond lover?') embodied the rakish elegance of Charles I's court.
stylistic_characteristics: Light, witty, conversational songs; a deliberately 'careless' aristocratic ease; satiric and bawdy verse; and dramatic prose and blank verse in his plays.
intellectual_concerns: Love and gallantry; wit and courtly fashion; royalist loyalty; sceptical libertinism; and the vanity of romantic pretence.
historical_significance: Suckling's lyrics and his legend as a doomed Cavalier made him an emblem of the Caroline court; his plays influenced Restoration comedy, and 'A Ballad upon a Wedding' is a lively social satire.
biographical_uncertainty: The exact circumstances of Suckling's death (suicide or accident) are uncertain and were debated even by contemporaries.

literary_identity: Poet and royalist administrator; author of Cooper's Hill (1642), the first great English topographical and reflective poem, whose balanced couplets established the model for Augustan nature-and-meditation verse.
biography: Born 1615 (baptised at St Andrew Holborn), educated at Trinity College, Oxford, and Lincoln's Inn. His tragedy The Sophy (1642) and Cooper's Hill (1642) won him immediate fame. A moderate royalist, he served Charles I and Charles II on diplomatic missions and as Surveyor of the King's Works (1660, after Inigo Jones), was knighted in 1660, and suffered a much-publicised bout of madness in 1666. He died in March 1669 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The poet of the meditative landscape, whose view of the Thames from Cooper's Hill yoked topography, history, and moral reflection in the balanced couplet that Pope praised as 'strong sense ... most correctly writ'.
stylistic_characteristics: The smooth, balanced closed couplet; topographical description as moral and political meditation; classical allusion; and a grave, sententious tone.
intellectual_concerns: Nature and order; the Thames, trade, and the English constitution; moderation and the 'golden mean'; royalist politics; and the relation of landscape to history and morality.
historical_significance: Cooper's Hill founded the English topographical and estate-mediation tradition that runs through Marvell, Pope ('Windsor-Forest'), and Thomson's Seasons, and its couplets shaped Augustan versification.
biographical_uncertainty: Denham's life is well documented, including his madness and the scandal of his wife's death; the dating of Cooper's Hill's revisions (1642, 1650, 1655, 1668) is established.

literary_identity: Cavalier poet and country parson; author of Hesperides (1648), a vast collection that joins pagan festivity, erotic lyrics, and devotional verse to a staunch Anglican and royalist piety rooted in rural Devon.
biography: Born August 1591 in London (baptised at St Vedast), educated at St John's College, Cambridge (BA 1617, then transferred). A 'Son of Ben' in the London wit circles, he took orders and was presented to the living of Dean Prior in Devon (1629), where he served — grumbling at the rustic parishioners — until ejected by Parliament in 1647 as a royalist. He returned to London, published Hesperides (1648) and the religious Noble Numbers, then was restored to Dean Prior in 1662 after the Restoration and lived there until his death in October 1674.
literary_profile: The poet of 'gather ye rosebuds while ye may', whose Hesperides celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of the English countryside with a classical gaiety shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith.
stylistic_characteristics: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics; classical and rustic imagery; a light, mellifluous metrical variety; and the pairing of pagan 'Hesperides' with the Christian 'Noble Numbers'.
intellectual_concerns: Carpe diem and mutability; rural festivity and custom; erotic love and marriage; Anglican ceremony and royalist loyalty; death and the consolations of faith.
historical_significance: Herrick is the greatest of the Cavalier lyricists in range and charm; Hesperides preserved the folklore and ceremonial culture of the English countryside and his lyrics have remained continuously popular.
biographical_uncertainty: Herrick's life is documented mainly through his own poems and parish records; his exact attitudes and the arrangement of Hesperides remain matters of interpretation.

literary_identity: Satirist and poet; author of Hudibras, the brilliant mock-heroic burlesque of Puritan hypocrisy that became one of the most quoted poems of the Restoration and defined English comic satire for a century.
biography: Born c. 1612–13 at Strensham, Worcestershire; educated at the free school of Worcester and possibly Cambridge. He served in Puritan and royalist households, acted as steward to the royalist Sir William Waller, and after the Restoration held posts including secretary to the Lord President of the Marches at Ludlow. He published Hudibras in three parts (1663, 1664, 1678), a huge success celebrated by the court but poorly rewarded; he left a mass of unpublished 'characters' and notes (printed posthumously as Miscellaneous Thoughts, 1759, and The Genuine Remains, 1694). He died in poverty on 25 September 1680.
literary_profile: The scourge of Puritan cant, whose Hudibras attacked the hypocrisy of the Presbyterian Independents in rollicking doggerel and proverbial wit, coining countless phrases still in use.
stylistic_characteristics: Comic octosyllabic couplets with absurd rhymes; mock-heroic and burlesque; a dense store of proverbs, puns, and learned-satiric allusion; and terse, epigrammatic 'characters' in prose.
intellectual_concerns: Hypocrisy, fanaticism, and false learning; royalist and Anglican loyalty; human folly and self-interest; and the satire of sectarian politics.
historical_significance: Hudibras was the most popular satire of the Restoration, a favourite of Charles II, and its mock-heroic technique directly influenced Dryden, Swift, and Pope's Dunciad.
biographical_uncertainty: Butler's birth year is approximate and his early life obscure; his later poverty and the posthumous publication of his remains are documented but partly traditional.

alternative_names: John Wilmot, Second Earl of Rochester
literary_identity: Libertine poet, courtier, and wit of Charles II's court; the greatest of the Restoration rakish versifiers, whose savage satires, bawdy lyrics, and bleak 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' combine intellectual rigour with scandalous candour.
biography: Born 1 April 1647 at Ditchley, Oxfordshire; educated at Burford and Wadham College, Oxford, then travelling in France and Italy. He became a favourite of Charles II, distinguished himself in the Second Dutch War (1665–66), and lived a notorious life of debauchery, abduction (of the heiress Elizabeth Malet, whom he married), imprisonment, and wit. His verse circulated largely in manuscript among the court wits; he wrote for the stage (a version of Valentinian, 1685) and translated Lucretius and Seneca. After a profound deathbed conversion under the bishop Gilbert Burnet, he died at Woodstock on 26 July 1680, aged 33. His Poems on Several Occasions appeared posthumously (1680).
literary_profile: The libertine philosopher-poet whose work interrogates reason, appetite, and human pretension with a cynical honesty and formal skill that modern critics rank among the finest of the age.
stylistic_characteristics: Biting satiric verse; the bawdy and obscene lyric; a philosophic bleakness and intellectual paradox; vigorous colloquial energy; and skilful use of the couplet and the song.
intellectual_concerns: Reason and appetite; the hypocrisy of civilization and court life; sexual libertinism; mortality and the vanity of human pride; and, at the last, repentance and faith.
historical_significance: Once dismissed as merely obscene, Rochester is now recognised as a serious and original satirist whose 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' is a major philosophic poem and whose influence extends to the modern revival of interest in Restoration libertinism.
biographical_uncertainty: Rochester's canon is unstable because most poems circulated anonymously in manuscript; attribution of individual verses is often uncertain and disputed.

alternative_names: Charles Sackville, Sixth Earl of Dorset
literary_identity: Courtier, patron, and occasional poet; as Lord Buckhurst he was a leading Restoration wit and rake, famed for his songs and satires, and later as Earl of Dorset a generous patron of Dryden, Prior, and the writers of the 1690s.
biography: Born c. 1643 (baptised 24 January 1638 — the commonly cited birth year is 1643; records vary), styled Lord Buckhurst, educated at Westminster. He served at sea against the Dutch (reportedly writing the song 'To all you ladies now at land' the night before the Battle of Lowestoft, 1665), was a boon companion of Rochester and the court wits, and succeeded as Earl of Dorset and Middlesex in 1675. After the Revolution of 1688 he became Lord Chamberlain to William III and a key literary patron, supporting Dryden after his fall, and Prior, and Montagu. He died 19 January 1706.
literary_profile: The elegant, careless court versifier whose few surviving songs and satires were praised by contemporaries (Prior, Dryden) for their natural wit and ease, and whose chief literary role was patronage.
stylistic_characteristics: Light, graceful songs and satires; an easy, natural wit; libertine and amorous subjects; and the occasional political satire.
intellectual_concerns: Love, pleasure, and court life; the passing of youth; loyalty and the politics of the Revolution; and the patronage of letters.
historical_significance: Dorset is remembered more as the ideal Restoration patron — Dryden dedicated works to him and mourned his circle — than for his slender but admired verse, which exemplifies Cavalier wit surviving into the 1690s.
biographical_uncertainty: Dorset's birth year is variously given (1637–38 or 1643); his poetic canon is small and some attributions are uncertain, and much of his reputation rests on testimony rather than surviving verse.

literary_identity: Poet and diplomat; a master of light verse, the burlesque, and the occasional poem, whose career under the patronage of Dorset and his diplomatic service produced the witty, polished poetry of the transition from Dryden to Pope.
biography: Born 21 July 1664 in London, educated at Westminster School (where, per legend, the Earl of Dorset discovered him reciting Horace) and St John's College, Cambridge. Patronised by Dorset, he entered diplomacy and government service under the Earls of Portland and the Tories, serving at the negotiations of the treaties of Ryswick (1697) and Utrecht (1713) and as a Commissioner of Customs. He wrote the burlesque 'The City Mouse and Country Mouse' (with Montagu, 1687), Solomon on the Vanity of the World (1718), Alma, and many songs, tales, and epistles. He died on 18 September 1721.
literary_profile: The poet of urbane lightness, whose easy, witty verse and translations made him one of the most popular poets between Dryden and Pope and a model for the familiar style.
stylistic_characteristics: Graceful octosyllabics and couplets; wit, irony, and colloquial ease; burlesque and mock-heroic; fable and tale; and a polished, Horatian lightness.
intellectual_concerns: Love and gallantry; the vanity of worldly ambition; politics and diplomacy; friendship and patronage; and moral philosophy in a light, Horatian key.
historical_significance: Prior's Poems on Several Occasions (1709) and later works were immensely popular; his light verse and translations helped form the Augustan taste and influenced Pope, who both admired and satirised him.
biographical_uncertainty: Prior's life is well documented, though the anecdotes of his discovery by Dorset are partly legendary; his diplomatic career is recorded in state papers.

literary_identity: Poet and translator, the first Englishwoman to achieve a significant public literary reputation and to have a play performed on the professional stage; celebrated as 'the Matchless Orinda' for her verse on female friendship and royalist loyalty.
biography: Born c. 1631–32 in London, daughter of a merchant; married the much older Philip Philips of Cardigan (1647) and lived at her estate of Owenia (Cardigan). There she formed a 'Society of Friendship', giving its members pastoral names (herself 'Orinda'), and wrote poems of idealised female friendship, love, and royalist politics. During the Interregnum she translated Corneille's Pompey and Horace, the first plays by a woman performed on the English public stage (1663). An unauthorised edition of her Poems appeared in 1664; she died of smallpox in London on 22 June 1664, and her collected Poems was published posthumously in 1667 to great acclaim.
literary_profile: The poet of virtuous female friendship and Cavalier loyalty, whose refined, platonic verse won her an unprecedented public reputation for a woman writer and made her a model for later women poets.
stylistic_characteristics: Polished couplets and songs; a chaste, platonic idealism; the rhetoric of friendship; and translations of French neoclassical drama in vigorous verse.
intellectual_concerns: Female friendship and virtue; retirement and the country life; royalist politics; the role of the woman writer; and the idealisation of platonic love.
historical_significance: Philips was the first Englishwoman to gain wide literary fame, to have her work printed (though against her wishes) and plays staged, and to be memorialised by Dryden and others as 'the Matchless Orinda' — a founding figure of women's professional authorship.
biographical_uncertainty: Philips's birth year is uncertain (1631 or 1632); the 1664 Poems was pirated and she disowned it, so the authoritative canon rests on the 1667 edition.

literary_identity: Poet and courtier; one of the finest women writers of the late seventeenth century, whose posthumously celebrated verse ranges from nature lyrics and the celebrated 'Nocturnal Reverie' to witty social poems and meditations on melancholy and her own precarious standing as a woman author.
biography: Born April 1661 at Sywell, educated and appointed maid of honour to Mary of Modena (wife of the Duke of York, later James II). She married Colonel Heneage Finch (1684); after James II's fall in 1688 the Finches were Jacobite exiles, and her husband's death (1689) plunged her into depression, which she wrote about candidly. When her brother-in-law became Earl of Winchilsea she became Countess of Winchilsea (1712). Her poems circulated in manuscript among a literary circle that included Pope and Swift; a collected Poems on Several Occasions appeared in 1713. She died on 5 August 1720.
literary_profile: The poet of sensuous nature, melancholy, and female authorship, whose 'Nocturnal Reverie' Wordsworth singled out as the finest nature poem between Milton and himself.
stylistic_characteristics: Mellifluous couplets and Pindaric forms; precise, sensuous nature description; candid treatments of depression ('The Spleen'); self-aware wit about being a woman writer; and translations from the French.
intellectual_concerns: Nature and contemplation; melancholy and the 'spleen'; the constraints on women's writing; Jacobite politics and exile; friendship; and religious resignation.
historical_significance: Long neglected, Finch was recovered by feminist criticism and is now recognised as a major poet of the period; her nature poetry influenced the Romantics and her verse on women's authorship ('The Introduction') is a key early feminist text.
biographical_uncertainty: Much of Finch's verse circulated in manuscript and its dating is often uncertain; her canon was substantially expanded by modern editions of her manuscripts.

literary_identity: The first published poet of the English colonies in America; a Puritan woman whose verse — 'The Tenth Muse' (1650) and later the intimate family and religious poems published from her manuscript — expresses both learned ambition and the domestic piety of New England.
biography: Born c. 1612 at Northampton, daughter of Thomas Dudley, steward to the Earl of Lincoln; exceptionally well educated. She married Simon Bradstreet (1628) and emigrated with him and her father to Massachusetts Bay on the Arbella (1630), where both husband and father served as governors. She bore eight children and wrote poetry amid the hardships of colonial life. Her brother-in-law published The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America (London, 1650) without her knowledge; a second, more personal collection appeared posthumously (Several Poems, 1678). She died on 16 September 1672 at Andover, Massachusetts.
literary_profile: The Puritan poet who reconciled learned ambition with humility, writing public 'quaternions' on the elements and the ages as well as tender poems to her husband, children, and house, all framed within a faith that submits worldly loss to God's will.
stylistic_characteristics: Formal 'quaternions' and duologues in the Du Bartas tradition; the intimate domestic lyric; self-deprecating prefaces that assert a woman's right to write; and a plain, heartfelt Puritan piety.
intellectual_concerns: Faith and submission to Providence; marriage, family, and motherhood; the place of the woman writer; loss, mortality, and the vanity of the world; and the New England experiment.
historical_significance: Bradstreet is the founding figure of American poetry and the first Englishwoman to publish a volume in the New World; her work documents Puritan inner life and women's experience and has been central to the recovery of early American and women's literature.
biographical_uncertainty: Bradstreet's exact birth year is uncertain (c. 1612); the dating of her manuscript poems and the authorship of some attributed pieces remain matters of scholarship.

literary_identity: Emblem-book poet and devotional writer; author of Emblems (1635), the most popular book of verse in seventeenth-century England, whose combination of picture, biblical motto, and moral verse made religious meditation accessible to a vast readership.
biography: Born 1592 at Romford, Essex, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge and Lincoln's Inn. He held minor offices under the crown, served as cupbearer to the Princess Elizabeth (the 'Winter Queen') at Heidelberg, and wrote a series of biblical paraphrases and religious poems (Esther, Job Militant, Divine Poems, 1620s–30s). His Emblems (1635) and Hieroglyphikes of the Life of Man (1638) were phenomenally popular. A royalist, he wrote pamphlets during the Civil Wars and died in London on 8 September 1644.
literary_profile: The master of the English emblem, whose illustrated moral verses blended Protestant devotion, common proverb, and baroque imagery for an enormous popular audience.
stylistic_characteristics: Emblem structure (picture, motto, epigram, verse); biblical paraphrase; a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely wit; and a mixture of learned allusion and popular appeal.
intellectual_concerns: Protestant devotion and moral instruction; the vanity of the world and the soul's pilgrimage; scripture and its paraphrase; and the edification of a lay readership.
historical_significance: Quarles's Emblems was arguably the bestselling English poem-book of the century and shaped popular religious imagination; though later critics (and Pope's 'the mob of gentlemen who wrote with ease') mocked him, his influence on Bunyan, the emblem tradition, and devotional culture was profound.
biographical_uncertainty: Quarles's life is documented in outline; his enormous popularity was later eclipsed by critical contempt, and the attribution of some anonymous emblem verses is uncertain.
